generated.script:
Hello. My name's Elena, and for the past four years I've been a volunteer with the Lakes Peak Mountain Rescue Team. People often imagine we're out climbing every weekend for fun, but most of what we do is training — because when a call comes in, there is no time to hesitate.

Before anyone is accepted, they have to pass an annual fitness test. It's not about being the fastest runner in the group; the instructors want to see that you can keep going uphill with a heavy pack for several hours without becoming a liability to the rest of the squad. After that, there's a basic background check, and only then do you join the trainee programme.

The programme starts in the classroom. New volunteers learn navigation — map reading, compass work, and how to describe a location accurately when you're speaking to the police or the ambulance service. I still remember my first night exercise in thick cloud on the lower slopes. I thought I knew the path, but without proper navigation training I would simply have walked in circles.

Every member carries a whistle, which sounds obvious, but in wind you can't rely on shouting. One short blast means "Where are you?" and two means "Come to me." We drill those signals until they're automatic, because on a ridge you may not be able to see the person ten metres ahead of you.

The initial course also includes an accredited first aid qualification. You're taught to treat hypothermia, stabilise a leg injury, and keep someone calm while you wait for professional paramedics. The certificate has to be renewed, so we run refreshers every spring.

Outdoor kit has to be fully waterproof — not shower-resistant, not "good enough for town," but capable of keeping you dry in horizontal rain above the treeline. The team publishes a kit list, and leaders check your bag before major exercises. Cheap gloves that soak through in twenty minutes are not acceptable.

When someone is seriously injured on a remote ridge, we request a helicopter from the national search service. The pilot cannot land on a narrow ledge, so we prepare a landing site lower down and carry the casualty on a stretcher to meet the aircraft. Those exercises are exhausting, but they teach you how much coordination a real rescue requires.

All team leaders are unpaid and work on a voluntary basis. Employers are generally supportive because they know the skills — leadership, communication, staying calm under pressure — transfer back to the workplace. Even so, balancing shift work with sudden call-outs at two in the morning is not easy.

Ropes are used most often on steep ground where a slip would have serious consequences. You learn to set up anchors, belay a colleague, and descend safely with a load. It's repetitive practice on the same rocky outcrop month after month until the procedures feel boring — and that's exactly the point.

Call-outs frequently happen in poor visibility. Fog, sleet, and darkness combine to turn a familiar path into something disorientating. GPS helps, but batteries fail and screens crack, so we still teach old-fashioned techniques with map and compass.

Many recruits tell me the training gave them greater confidence in the mountains. Not arrogance — you never stop respecting the weather — but a quiet belief that if something went wrong, you would know what to do first, who to contact, and how to keep yourself and others safe until help arrives.
